name: The Lantern Causeway
unique_feature: a boardwalk of lantern poles lit each dusk by a lamplighter who sings as she goes
story: The lamplighter Lissane has walked it for forty years. When she is late the boardwalk is not safe, and she is late on purpose when she wants Isseva to notice her.
encounter: bog-drowned climb the poles after dark if the lanterns are out

name: Drowned Bell Shrine
unique_feature: a Hearthstone on a peat island above a bell that tolls once at midnight from under the water
story: The reedfolk bury their dead with lanterns; the bell is older than any of them and nobody buried it.
encounter: none; wisps circle at midnight

name: The Sallow King
unique_feature: a willow so old its branches have rooted again in a ring, making a hall of trunks
story: Sallowjaws nest under its roots and the reedfolk feed them so they nest nowhere else. It is the only place in the marsh where you are asked not to kill anything.
encounter: sallowjaw ambush from the water inside the ring; a moral choice with reputation cost

name: The Reed Wreck
unique_feature: a Salt Isles trading ship stranded three miles inland among the reeds
story: No flood on record could have carried it here. The reedfolk say the Tide came in once, briefly, and went out again; the ship's log stops the day before.
encounter: leech-hounds in the hold; a chart of the Salt Isles

name: The Stair of Isse
unique_feature: a sunken Oroth colonnade rising step by step out of the water toward the Drowned Nave
story: The Builders' processional way. The reedfolk call it Isse's Stair and say the Named woman walked down it into the water to teach the stilts.
encounter: bog-drowned rise from between the columns as you pass; fight on the steps, not in the water

name: Wisp Hollow
unique_feature: a dead-end channel where wisps gather over a drowned house whose chimney still stands
story: The family's lanterns were never lit for them; the wisps are what a water-burial becomes when nobody sings.
encounter: wisps lure toward deep water; silence them or ignore their light; a strongbox in the chimney

name: The Tideflat Stones
unique_feature: three stones on the sea's edge marking a shoreline that no longer exists
story: The soft western edge. Beyond them the flats go grey and the Salt Isles are a rumour. A survey point for the western chart.
encounter: none; crabs

name: Heron Watch
unique_feature: a reedfolk lookout on tall stilts with a bittern nesting in its bell
story: The watch was raised to see the Lakefolk coming for the weir. Now it is where young reedfolk go to be alone together.
encounter: none; a vista over the delta

name: The Fog Bell
unique_feature: a stilt-tower with a fog-bell rung every quarter hour while the fog is down, so the eel-boats can find the channel
story: The ringer is paid in eels by Moreva and Isseva both, and rings through the night whenever the fog is in, which is most nights. When the bell stops, the boats come in to find out why.
encounter: none
hook: The Fog Bell stopped last night, and the ringer is not in the tower.

name: The Long Jetty
unique_feature: a burial boardwalk running out into Lissane Mere, its last post hung with lanterns for the unmourned
story: Isseva buries its own from the town jetty. The Long Jetty is for the drowned who come up without a name; the reedfolk light a lantern for each and sing the third voice of the round.
encounter: bog-drowned climb to the last post at midnight
hook: Somebody has been leaving lanterns with names on them at the Long Jetty, and the names are all from the Vale.

name: The Peat Hags
unique_feature: a peat-cutters' camp on a drying island, the turves stacked like loaves around the fire
story: Peat from the south marsh warms Isseva, Nauve's Landing and half of Tollmere's poorer streets. The cutters find things in the peat, and are paid more for the finding than for the peat.
encounter: leech-hounds come up to the cuttings after dark
hook: The cutters have dug up a Warden, perfectly kept, with a roll of names in his hand; the Wardens and the Order both want him.

name: The Drowned Arch
unique_feature: an Oroth arch standing at the edge of Mormere with nothing on either side of it
story: The reedfolk say the arch was a door and the marsh was a room. Eel-boats pass under it for luck, and never through it the other way.
encounter: none
hook: An eel-boat went through the Drowned Arch the wrong way and came out at dawn with its crew a day older than they should be.

name: The Sunken Tower
unique_feature: a Builders' tower drowned to its third course, whose roof the reedfolk children dive from
story: Once a watch over a shore that is a mile out to sea now. The children dive from the top to touch the fourth course, which is carved with a face.
encounter: sallowjaws bask on the drowned courses
hook: The face carved on the fourth course is the face of the Thirteenth colossus.

name: The Traders' Post
unique_feature: the beach where Salt Isles traders drew up their boats and traded charts for indigo, their tent-poles still standing in the sand
story: The traders came every midsummer for three hundred years and stopped forty years ago without a word. Oulea still puts up one tent for them on the longest day.
encounter: none
hook: This midsummer a trader's chart was pinned to a tent-pole, and there was no boat on the sea.

name: The Eel-Boat Graveyard
unique_feature: eel-boats left to rot on the flats where the reedfolk say the drowned come ashore to count them
story: A reedfolk boat is never broken up; when it is done it is brought here and left to the tide. There are three hundred of them, and some of them have moved in the night.
encounter: bog-drowned walk among the hulls at night
hook: Ollo Nauve built one of the boats that moved, and wants it back where he left it.

name: Crookstilts
unique_feature: a hut on crooked stilts in the carr where the marsh-hag trades cures for names
story: The marsh-hag cures anything and takes a name in payment, not your own, one you know. The reedfolk go to her anyway, and do not say whose names they gave.
encounter: leech-hounds guard the stilts after dark
hook: The marsh-hag has Tessane's name, and will trade it.

name: The Indigo Beds
unique_feature: Isseva's north dye beds, where cloth is steeped in marsh indigo in long reed troughs
story: The only indigo in Wickmere comes up in these beds. This year it is coming up pale, and the dyers blame the fog, and Loa Oul blames the drowned.
encounter: none; dyers with jobs going
hook: Find out where the indigo's colour is going: the dyers have noticed the pale beds are the ones nearest the Nave.

name: The Round Stones
unique_feature: three stones on three peat islets where the Round of Sa'oul is sung at midsummer, a choir on each
story: The round goes from stone to stone across the water, each voice starting as the last reaches the third line. It does not end; somebody stops, and then somebody else.
encounter: none
hook: Sing the second voice slightly flat on the fourth line and an old woman on the far islet begins to weep.

name: Mor'oul
unique_feature: a stilt-village sunk in a flood nobody recorded, its roof-ridges just under the water
story: The reedfolk put the drowned's apostrophe into its name the year it went under. The Tide account says a flood; there has never been a flood in any record, except here, in the name.
encounter: bog-drowned at their own doors
hook: Under the water Mor'oul's own lanterns are still lit.

name: Oskel Ford
unique_feature: an Oroth footbridge of column-drums laid across the Oskel where it comes down out of the heights into the fen
story: The only dry way from the clans' Oskeld Dale into the fen. Oskel miners carry lead down it to trade at Isseva, and the reedfolk never cross it the other way.
encounter: none
hook: Ore-carts have been found in the fen with the silver still aboard and the carters gone, and the Oskel clan want the ford watched.

name: Saoul
unique_feature: a ring of empty stilts standing in a black pool, a lit lantern hung on every one
story: The lantern-pool, named for Sa'oul, who is in it. The village that stood here moved to Saeva a hundred years ago and left its lanterns for her.
encounter: wisps over the pool at night
hook: The lanterns are relit every night, and the reedfolk swear that none of them does it.

name: The Greyreed Decoy
unique_feature: a wildfowlers' decoy of netted channels cut into the reeds, with a screen of wattle for the decoyman
story: Nauvissa's decoyman draws the Greyreed's ducks up the netted pipes with a dog and a song. He sells every bird to Tollmere and eats none of them.
encounter: none; a decoyman and his dog
hook: The decoy dog has started leading something else up the pipes at night, and the nets are torn from inside.

name: The Salt Pans
unique_feature: square brine pools on the tideflats drying white in rows, and the salt-rakers' huts on legs
story: The only salt in Wickmere that is not carried down from the Skerrow mines. The reedfolk trade it for lamp-oil and say the sea is giving back what it owes.
encounter: none; salt-rakers
hook: A pan dried to a crust overnight with footprints across it from the sea side, and none coming back.

name: The Tide Hearth
unique_feature: a Hearthstone on the Outfall's south bank hung round with lantern-knots, one for every name the water has taken
story: Reedfolk who have lost someone to the water come here to tie a knot and say the name once. The Sayers call it superstition; the Tallymen charge nothing to pass it, which is the most respect Tollmere has.
encounter: none
hook: A knot has been tied for a name nobody in Sedgemire knows, and it stays dry in the spray.

name: The Old Crannog
unique_feature: an island-house of wattle on a heap of stones in the carr, older than any stilt in Sedgemire
story: The reedfolk say their grandmothers' grandmothers lived on islands before Isse taught them stilts. The crannog is the last one, and nobody sleeps in it twice.
encounter: leech-hounds in the carr at night
hook: Somebody has been sleeping in it every night, and leaves the fire laid for the next.

name: The Knuckle Cairn
unique_feature: a clan cairn on the last dry stone before the fen, capped with a giant's knuckle-bone
story: The Oskel clan's boundary. Past it, the clans say, is not their memory's business.
encounter: none
hook: The knuckle-bone has been turned to point into the fen, which in clan sign means follow.

name: The Drowned Road
unique_feature: an Oroth road of fused stone running straight out of the carr and into the sea
story: The Builders' road west, cut off where the sea took the land. The reedfolk say it goes on under the water to the Salt Isles, and the Salt Isles traders say it arrives.
encounter: none
hook: At the lowest tide this spring the road showed a milestone further out than anyone had seen, cut with a number.

name: The Grey Gull
unique_feature: a Salt Isles trading ship driven onto the carr's edge, her figurehead a gull with a woman's face
story: She came ashore in the storm of 1031 with nobody aboard and her boats still lashed. The reedfolk have taken nothing from her, because a ship that comes without its crew has come for someone.
encounter: none
hook: The figurehead's face has been recognised: a reedfolk woman of Moreva, alive, who has never been to sea.

name: The Boardwalk Gate
unique_feature: a reedfolk gate of lantern-hung posts where the Westway leaves the downs and goes onto a boardwalk over the delta
story: Nauvissa keeps the gate and lights it every dusk, so that the Vale's carters know where the ground stops.
encounter: none
hook: The lanterns were found lit at noon, and the boardwalk wet with footprints coming out of the delta.

name: The Reed Bridge
unique_feature: a footbridge of bundled reed over a creek, a new one laid on the old every spring
story: Nobody has taken the old bridge down in two hundred years; the reedfolk lay the new one on top, and the bridge stands higher every year.
encounter: none
hook: The bridge has sunk to the water overnight, two hundred years of reed pressed flat as if something very heavy had crossed.

name: The Eel Hurdles
unique_feature: the eel-trappers' summer raft of huts moored among wattle hurdles that steer the eels into the traps
story: Oulea's trappers live out on the water from thaw to first frost and come ashore only for burials.
encounter: none; eel-trappers
hook: Every morning the traps are full of eels swimming the wrong way, out to sea.

name: The Cockle Beds
unique_feature: the tideflats' cockle-beds staked out in family rows, each stake tied with its family's lantern-knot
story: The reedfolk rake the beds at low water. A stake moved in the night has started more feuds in Sedgemire than eels have.
encounter: none; cockle-rakers at low water
hook: Every stake on the beds was found moved one row toward the sea.

name: The Withy Beds
unique_feature: osier-beds cut to stools in rows, where the reedfolk grow the withies for their eel-traps
story: Nauve's Landing weaves every eel-trap in Sedgemire from these withies, and the beds are older than the Landing.
encounter: none; withy-cutters
hook: The withies have grown a yard since the new moon, and every one of them has grown toward the Mere.

name: The South Stilts
unique_feature: a reedfolk watch-house on stilts at the delta's southern edge, looking out over the grey
story: Nauvissa raised it in the Ash Winter to see the grey coming. The watchman is paid in eels and has not seen it move in twenty years.
encounter: none
hook: The watchman says the grey has started coming in at night and going back by day, and nobody believes him.

name: The Eel Stews
unique_feature: stone-walled ponds in the fen where live eels are kept for the Tollmere market, one pond walled higher than the rest
story: Nauve's Landing sells its eels alive: a dead eel is a Tallyman's price and a live one is a reedfolk's.
encounter: none
hook: The high-walled pond has been found empty with its sluice shut, and its wall is wet on the outside.

name: The Lantern-Wright's Camp
unique_feature: a reedfolk lantern-maker's camp on a peat hummock beside the Westway, horn panes drying on a rack by the fire
story: Every lantern hung on the Boardwalk Gate and every lantern sunk with the reedfolk's dead is made here, from horn scraped thin enough to read through. The lantern-wright sings rounds while she works, alone, taking every part herself.
encounter: wisps gather at the drying racks after dark, drawn by the horn panes
hook: Every lantern made here this month has come out with its flame burning downward, toward the water.

name: The Lead-Carriers' Rest
unique_feature: a lead-carriers' stopping place at the edge of the fen below Oskel Ford, pack frames stacked beside the fire and a lantern pole marking the dry path
story: Oskel miners carry their lead down out of the dale to trade at Isseva, and rest here before the fen. The reedfolk never cross the ford the other way, and the miners never ask them to; the rest is the one place both stand.
encounter: leech-hounds come up the fen edge at dusk
hook: The reedfolk have started leaving a lantern lit on the pole for the Oskel carriers, which the reedfolk do for nobody who is not drowned.

name: The Drowned Byre
unique_feature: the roofless stone byre of a farm the fen came up over, one gable standing out of the reeds of the Carr
story: There was dry pasture on this edge of the fen before the Mere fell and the delta spread, and a clan family kept cattle here, the only clan folk who ever farmed on the flat. The fen came up a hand a year until the byre stood in it, and they drove the beasts up the dale and never came back down.
encounter: bog-drowned climb out of the Carr after dark
hook: Cattle have been heard lowing in the byre at night, and in the morning there is fresh dung on a floor the water has covered for forty years.

name: The Lantern Hummock
unique_feature: a peat island shrine by the North Channel causeway, lantern poles round a stone and an old bell just under the water beside it
story: The reedfolk bury their dead in the water with a lantern. For the ones the water took and did not give back, there is no burial, so a lantern is lit for them here on the hummock, on the one night each year that it can be seen from Moreva.
encounter: none
hook: A lantern has been lit on the hummock for somebody who is still alive, and the reedfolk will not say whose.

name: The Settled House
unique_feature: the roofless stilt-house of a Moreva family whose stilts rotted under it, the house settled down onto the peat with one gable still standing
story: When a stilt-house's stilts rot the reedfolk do not rebuild it. They say the house has come down to meet the water, and the family moves, and the house is left to wait for the flood the Tide account promises. The family's eel-spear lies across the beams, where they can reach it if the water comes before they are ready.
encounter: bog-drowned climb onto the beams after dark
hook: The family has come back to live in it, sitting up on the gable and the beams, waiting, they say, for the water to come up and take them out to where it went.

name: The Pushers' Stones
unique_feature: three leaning stones on the bank below the Eelweir, where whoever was pushed off the weir each autumn climbs out and leans to dry
story: Reedfolk and Lakefolk share the Eelweir by an agreement neither side has read, and every autumn one of them pushes one of the other into the Outfall. The stones are where the pushed climb out and lean, dripping, and are handed a cup by the pusher, which is also the agreement.
encounter: none
hook: This autumn nobody was pushed in, for the first time in anyone's memory, and both sides are frightened of what that means.

name: The Broken Stilts
unique_feature: a ring of broken stilts beside the Isseva causeway where a platform stood, the water round them black and still
story: A reedfolk family's fishing platform stood here until a sallowjaw took the stilts out from under it one at a time. The reedfolk did not rebuild. They say the sallowjaw waited forty years for the platform to be worth taking, and has earned the ring.
encounter: a sallowjaw waits in the black water by the stilts
hook: The broken stilts have been found capped with lit lanterns, one for each of the family who lived on the platform, though none of them died there.

name: The Drowned Road Post
unique_feature: a tall lantern pole with indigo rags on the North Fen's safe way to the Drowned Road, its lantern kept lit at dusk
story: The fen round the Drowned Road will take a walker who strays a stride off the hard ground, so the reedfolk mark the safe way with lantern poles, and this is the last before the old road. Its lantern is lit at dusk by whoever passes last.
encounter: none
hook: The lantern has been found lit at dusk and burning under the water, a stride off the safe way, where no hand could have set it.

name: The Peat-Cutters' Light
unique_feature: a lantern pole hung with indigo rags on the Delta's peat, marking the cutters' way home through the fog
story: The peat-cutters work the hags out on the Delta where the fog comes down in an hour, and walk home by the lantern poles. This is the pole the whole way is counted from: from here the Landing's lights can be seen.
encounter: none
hook: The cutters came home through the fog last week and counted one pole more on the way than there has ever been.

name: The Eel-Smoker's Hut
unique_feature: a cone of poles thatched with reed on the Delta's edge by the Westway, smoke seeping through its thatch where eels are hung to cure
story: An old reedfolk woman smokes eels in a reed hut on the dry edge of the Delta, where the Vale's carters meet the boardwalk, and sells them to both sides at one price, which she says is the only fair thing on the Westway.
encounter: none
hook: She has started smoking eels for somebody who comes at night and pays in the Vale's old pennies, the kind with the Toll whole on them.

name: The Drowned Trader
unique_feature: a trading ship sunk to her rails in the Delta's mud beside the Saeva road, her mast leaning, indigo rags tied to the shrouds
story: A Lakefolk trader came up the Delta too far on a spring tide and settled in the mud when it ran out. The reedfolk tied indigo to her shrouds to mark her for the boats, and say that what went down with her crew still keeps her.
encounter: the drowned rise from the hull after dark
hook: The indigo rags on the shrouds have been untied in the night and tied again in the Lakefolk's knot.

name: The Unsung Vault
unique_feature: a black Oroth doorway sunk to its lintel in a peat hummock of the carr, its approach lined with lantern poles whose lanterns are all cold
story: The Builders cut a cistern under the carr and the carr grew over it. When the reedfolk found it they gave it the drowned nobody could sing for: the ones who came up nameless, the ones whose people were all gone. Their lanterns were carried down and kept lit by a Keeper who sang the whole round for all of them, every night, one Keeper after another for three hundred years. This winter the singing under the carr stopped, and the lanterns on the poles went out one by one from the door outward.
encounter: the drowned wait on the steps of the doorway after dark; inside, the unsung who were never sung for, and the last Keeper at the bottom, still holding her lantern
hook: A knot-cord hangs from the lintel in the Keepers' weave: one knot for every Keeper, and the last knot has been tied and then pulled half undone.

site.hook_prompt: Read the knot-cord on the lintel

name: Greylag Fold
unique_feature: a round withy fold on a dry rise of the North Fen full of grey geese, the goose-herd's stilt-house beside it and her punt drawn up under it
story: The Mors have wintered the grey geese on the North Fen since before the Nave leaned. The geese come down from the clans' country in the first frost and the family brings them in to the fold at dusk by singing, because a goose will follow a round it has heard since the egg. Since the singing under the carr stopped, the geese will not settle; they face west all night, toward the Vault, and call.
encounter: leech-hounds come up out of the carr after the geese at night
hook: The old goose-herd sits up all night on her deck with a lantern, singing the third voice of the round, because, she says, somebody has to.

name: The Stakes at Oulnauve
unique_feature: a palisade of black bog-oak stakes on a peat island where the deep channel bends, its yard heaped with burial lanterns cut from the water, every one unlit
story: The Tide account says the water went out and will come back, and that when it does the drowned will walk ashore. The Flood-Callers are the reedfolk who got tired of waiting for it. They cut the burial lanterns off the water before they can burn down, so that the dead go out with nothing to steer by and come back up, and they call each one that rises a wave of the flood. They have built their stakes where the Oulnauve channel bends, and they have a great many lanterns.
encounter: Flood-Callers on the fighting step and the watch platforms; the Caller, Aunsa Mor, in the yard among the lanterns, and the drowned they have raised penned in the ditch
hook: A burial lantern nailed to the gate by its frame, and on the frame, in fresh indigo, the Callers' mark: a wave, and under it the words THEY ARE COMING HOME.

site.hook_prompt: Look at the lantern nailed to the gate

name: The Eel Tally
unique_feature: a Tallymen's counting-house on stilts at the head of the stews' channel, the Guild's brass lantern over the door and the eel-barrels ranked below it in chalked rows
story: Every live eel that goes up to Tollmere from the Delta is counted at the Tally first, and one in ten stays behind as the Guild's. The reedfolk pole their catch in, the clerk chalks it on the barrels and in the book, and a hired bravo sits on the steps with his hand on his hilt in case anybody counts differently. The clerk this year is new, and he has noticed that the book and the barrels do not agree.
encounter: the Guild's bravo sits on the tally-house steps by day and fights anyone who touches the barrels
hook: One row of barrels has been chalked twice, in two hands, and the numbers do not match.

name: Hester's House
unique_feature: a Vale cottage of lime-washed wattle and thatch set down on a peat island in the reeds, with a barley patch no bigger than a boat and a row of named lanterns on its fence
story: Hester Wrenn came down the Westway from Gosford forty years ago behind a reedman who had come up it selling eels, and he built her a house the way they build them in the Vale so that she would stay. He went into the water twenty years ago and she stayed anyway. She is the only person in Sedgemire who grows barley and the only one who knows the names of the Vale folk the marsh has drowned, because they come to her door first.
encounter: none; a widow who talks to strangers, and a fence of lanterns
hook: One lantern on her fence has no name on it, and she will not say whose it is until somebody asks.

name: Isse's Chair
unique_feature: a ring of nine black stilts of bog-oak, turned to stone at the foot, round a low seat of green Oroth stone heaped with cut reeds and knots
story: The reedfolk say these are the legs of Isse's own house, the first ever built on stilts, and that the seat is where she sat to teach the others how. Couples are married standing between two of the stilts with a reed held between them; the dead are named here before they are sent out. The stilts are older than Isseva, and the seat is Builders' work older than that, and nobody can say who put the one inside the other.
encounter: none; the Chair's tender, and what people leave
hook: Somebody has left a knot on the seat tied in no weave any lantern-maker knows, and it has not rotted in a month of rain.

name: The Leech-Wife's Stilts
unique_feature: a stilt-house over a ring of sunken leech-tubs and empty wattle kennels, a pole of iron collars hung by the door
story: Illa Nauve keeps the leeches Isseva's bleeders use, and she kept the hounds that were bred to guard them: sleek marsh dogs that learned from the leeches how to drink. Last spring the hounds went into the reeds after her old bitch and did not come back, and now they come back every night, and hunt the tubs, and her.
encounter: leech-hounds circle the tubs after dark, the old bitch that leads them among them
hook: The collar pole has one hook empty and scratched bright, as if something had been pulling at it from below.

name: The Draining Mill
unique_feature: a Tollmere windmill with torn sails standing on the open delta, built to pump the marsh dry, its sluice gate choked with reeds and black water
story: Forty years ago the Tallymen bought the rights to the west Delta from the Reed Council for a boat of silver and built a wind-pump to drain it for sheep. It pumped for one summer. The water it lifted out of the ground was not the marsh's water, the Oulea folk say, but something older from underneath, and the engineer went down into the sump to see why it tasted of iron, and the mill has not turned since.
encounter: bog-drowned rise from the sump after dark and walk the dry channel the mill cut
hook: The engineer's pumping-book is still on the ledge by the sluice, open at the last day, with a column of figures that goes wrong halfway down.

name: The Drylanders' Hummock
unique_feature: a low green hummock west of Isseva crowded with earth graves, each marked with a board in a stranger's letters and, beside it, a reedfolk lantern pole
story: The reedfolk give their dead to the water. People from the dry country do not want to go into the water, and say so, and Isseva has always listened: the Tallymen's clerks, the Vale carters, a Warden or two and a Salt Isles sailor are buried here in the earth the way they asked. The reedfolk did not know what else a grave wanted, so each one has a lantern as well.
encounter: wisps come to the lanterns at midnight, when nobody from the dry country is there to light them
hook: The newest board is a Vale name, cut last month, and there is nobody under it.

name: The Bog-Iron Bloomery
unique_feature: a squat clay furnace smoking on a hummock among flooded ore-pits, heaps of rust-red bog ore and charcoal round it and the slag in black rivers down the bank
story: The only iron the reedfolk have is the iron the marsh makes: red ore that grows in the pits a hand's depth a lifetime. The Lissas dig it and smelt it here in a clay bloomery they build again every spring, and every eel-spear and boat-nail in the Delta came out of it. The pits they dug when their grandmothers were girls have filled with water again, and the sallowjaws have found them warm from the furnace.
encounter: sallowjaws lie in the flooded ore-pits and come up at whoever walks the pit edges
hook: The bloomer's tally-cord hangs from the furnace with this spring's blooms knotted on it, and it stops a month ago.

name: The Grey Line
unique_feature: rows of withy stakes driven across the reed-beds south of Nauvissa, one row for every year, each tagged with a knot; beyond the last row the reeds are the colour of ash
story: Every midsummer since the Ash Winter, Nauvissa has walked south to where the reeds go grey and driven a row of stakes along the edge of it, and tied that year's knot to each one. There are sixty rows. The oldest are far in the grey now, their knots gone white; the newest is a reed-bed from the village. Nobody has ever had to move a row back, and this spring, for the first time, the grey has come in past the new row at night and gone back by day.
encounter: at night the grey comes in over the rows, and what walks in it walks with it
hook: The newest row's knots have been tied again in the night, in grey rush, by somebody who knew the weave.
